insights.title: Cabin ventilation is the worst case, not a safety margin
insights.answer: Rate materials and plan fire response for airflow near 10 cm/s, the speed of spacecraft ventilation, because that is where solids burn at the lowest oxygen and spread fastest.
insights.explanation: Still-air tests made microgravity look safer, but a gentle airflow feeds a flame with fresh oxygen without the cooling that strong buoyant flow brings on Earth [F-003]. NASA's review places the lowest oxygen limit for flame spread at about 10 cm/s, the typical ventilation speed, where spread is also fastest [F-008]. BASS-II traced a U-shaped boundary, with flames going out at both very low and high flow [F-017], and BASS showed spread responding immediately to flow changes [F-015].
insights.recommendation: Test candidate cabin materials in microgravity-relevant flows (around 10 cm/s), not only in still air or 1 g upward burning, and include ventilation control in fire procedures.
insights.caveats: The 10 cm/s minimum is a review-level result for flame spread over solids; it was not measured at Moon or Mars gravity. Russian Mir work and NASA's review differ on what switching ventilation off achieves [F-030, F-010].

insights.title: After a fire, toxic gas is the main threat
insights.answer: Size detection and cleanup for carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide first: in large spacecraft fire tests, gas build-up mattered more than heat or pressure.
insights.explanation: Saffire VI found the rise in CO2 and CO more significant than the temperature and pressure rise inside the Cygnus spacecraft [F-020]. Saffire IV and V fires reached 10 kW yet kept average cabin conditions acceptable [F-019]. BASS-II flames burned fuel-rich with CO to CO2 ratios ten times those of efficient combustion [F-016], and the 1997 Mir fire filled the station with smoke that took hours to clear [F-031].
insights.recommendation: Carry CO and CO2 sensing and post-fire atmosphere cleanup sized for a multi-kilowatt fire, and give crews masks they can reach in seconds.
insights.caveats: Saffire tests were uncrewed, in one vehicle size (17–19 m³) and at ISS-like air; results at 34 % O₂ or in partial gravity are not available.

insights.title: More oxygen demands stricter material control
insights.answer: Treat any cabin above 21 % oxygen as a higher fire risk and tighten material and ignition-source rules to match.
insights.explanation: Crewed spacecraft always contain fuel, oxygen and ignition sources, often at a higher oxygen fraction than air, with little room to escape [F-013]. In Apollo 1, pure oxygen at 16.7 psi and too much flammable material let a fire spread very rapidly [F-032]. On Mir, an oxygen generator itself was the fire source [F-031].
insights.recommendation: For 34 % O₂ exploration habitats, re-qualify materials at that oxygen level and treat oxygen-generating hardware as a fire source in hazard analyses.
insights.caveats: Apollo 1 and Mir are single incident reports, not controlled tests; the exploration atmosphere's flammability is not quantified by these findings.

insights.title: Moon gravity may make some materials more flammable
insights.answer: Do not assume lunar gravity is safer than Earth: for some materials it extends flammability, so lunar habitats and landers need their own material data.
insights.explanation: Lunar gravity removes much of the convective cooling but still drives enough buoyant flow to bring oxygen to a flame, a 'goldilocks zone' that raises flammability limits for some materials [F-028]. A cotton-fiberglass fabric that goes out immediately on Earth keeps burning downward at lunar gravity [F-029]. NASA's review notes that in low flow, in microgravity or partial gravity, some materials burn at lower oxygen than in 1 g [F-004].
insights.recommendation: Fly or simulate lunar-gravity flammability tests (as FM2 plans) at the habitat atmospheres, including 34 % O₂ at 8.2 psia, before certifying materials.
insights.caveats: Evidence comes from centrifuge, parabolic-flight and review statements; long-duration lunar tests have not flown yet. Mars gravity (0.38 g) is untested in these findings. FLEX droplet tests also stopped at 0.70 atm, above the 8.2 psia (about 0.56 atm) exploration air [F-036].

insights.title: Earth material tests are not conservative for space
insights.answer: Add a safety margin to, or replace, 1 g material ratings for space use, because several lines of evidence show materials can burn in space where Earth tests say they won't.
insights.explanation: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 is an upward-burning 1 g test, and drop-tower results suggest it might not be conservative [F-018]. Droplet flammability limits are lower in reduced gravity [F-001], some solids burn at lower oxygen in low flow [F-004], and on Earth a flame's own buoyant flow (at least about 30 cm/s) makes slow-flow behaviour impossible to test [F-027]. Designers have had to rely on 1 g understanding for lack of large-scale space data [F-021]. FLEX's own report also found droplet oxygen limits slightly lower than expected before flight [F-033].
insights.recommendation: Use microgravity flammability data (e.g., FLARE, SoFIE) to set oxygen margins on Test 1 results, and develop 1 g tests that can estimate microgravity limits: a blowoff-based rod test estimated 13.4 % O₂ for PMMA against 13.6 % observed in BASS-II [F-039].
insights.caveats: The size of the margin needed is not established by these findings; it differs by material and flow.

insights.title: Switching off ventilation will not reliably put a fire out
insights.answer: Use ventilation shutdown as one tool, not as the fire-fighting plan: still air in microgravity does not guarantee a fire goes out.
insights.explanation: NASA lists 'a fire will self-extinguish if ventilation is shut off' among disproved misconceptions [F-010]. Candles burned for up to 45 minutes in still air on Mir [F-024]. Russian Mir researchers proposed lowering or stopping ventilation as a fire-safety concept [F-030], and very low flow can extinguish flames on solids [F-017], so the outcome depends on the material and how still the air really is.
insights.recommendation: Keep active suppression available even after ventilation is stopped, and confirm extinction visually and with gas sensors.
insights.caveats: The findings disagree in emphasis: Mir work favours ventilation control [F-030], NASA's review warns against relying on it [F-010].

insights.title: Smoke detectors must be built for space smoke
insights.answer: Design and test spacecraft smoke detectors for microgravity smoke particles (mostly 200–400 nm), not for Earth smoke.
insights.explanation: Microgravity flames produce very different particle sizes, so an Earth detector would be looking for the wrong signature [F-011]. SAME-2 measured smoke from overheated spacecraft materials at mostly 200–400 nm, larger in still air [F-022]. Smoke onset in low gravity differs from earlier predictions [F-012], and cool flames can keep reacting with no visible flame [F-002].
insights.recommendation: Qualify detectors against microgravity smoke data and combine particle sensing with gas sensing (e.g., CO) to catch smouldering and cool-flame stages.
insights.caveats: SAME-2 tested five materials heated below ignition, not flaming fires; detector performance itself is not reported in these findings.

insights.title: Extinguishers can fail or feed a fire if misused
insights.answer: Train crews to aim suppressants for microgravity flames and use agents chosen for space, because a poorly aimed jet can strengthen a fire.
insights.explanation: In BASS, a nitrogen jet could entrain oxygen and make a flame stronger [F-014]. FLEX showed flammability limits are lower in reduced gravity, so Earth standards for inert-gas suppressants leave less margin [F-001]. NASA has moved to water-mist portable extinguishers on the ISS, replacing CO2 units [F-023].
insights.recommendation: Include microgravity suppression behaviour in extinguisher design and crew training, and size inert-gas quantities with reduced-gravity limits.
insights.caveats: The nitrogen effect is an early BASS observation; water-mist performance numbers are not part of these findings.

insights.title: Ignition is easier in low gravity
insights.answer: Tighten limits on hot surfaces and electrical faults, because materials ignite faster and with less heat in low gravity.
insights.explanation: Without buoyancy, less heat is carried off a material's surface, so it ignites more easily [F-005]. In slow airflow, ignition times were well below 1 g values and the critical heat flux can be as low as half [F-009]. Radiant heat from outside makes materials ignite and spread faster [F-007].
insights.recommendation: Lower allowed surface temperatures and heat fluxes near flammable materials, and keep separation from heaters and electronics.
insights.caveats: The half-heat-flux value comes from a model supported by short aircraft tests; long-duration confirmation is pending.

insights.title: Fires can spread upwind toward the air supply
insights.answer: Place detectors and plan suppression for flames that may spread against the airflow, toward vents, not only downstream.
insights.explanation: In slow microgravity airflow a flame on a thin fuel spreads upstream into the oncoming air, the opposite of Earth [F-006]. BASS showed flame spread reacting quickly and strongly to changes in flow [F-015].
insights.recommendation: Model spread in both directions for cabin layouts and position sensors near ventilation inlets as well as outlets.
insights.caveats: Upstream spread was shown for thin fuels at low flow speeds; thick materials and partial gravity are not covered.

insights.title: A fire that looks out may not be out
insights.answer: Confirm extinction with sensors and time, because dim, oscillating or invisible flames can persist in microgravity.
insights.explanation: FLEX droplets kept burning in invisible cool flames after the visible flame died [F-002]. Candle flames oscillated for up to a minute before going out [F-025] and burned for up to 45 minutes when oxygen allowed [F-024]. SOFBALL's flame balls burned at about 1 watt for over 40 minutes [F-026].
insights.recommendation: Add a post-fire watch period with gas and particle monitoring before declaring a fire out.
insights.caveats: These phenomena come from small droplet, candle and premixed-gas experiments; their relevance to large material fires is inferred.
